hints: Remember that hydrolysis with aqueous NaOH is alkaline hydrolysis, so think about what two types of product an ester always gives under these conditions.
Split the ester $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2(\text{CH}_2)_7\text{CH}_3$ at the $\text{CO}_2$ link to find the acid part $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2$ and the alcohol part $(\text{CH}_2)_7\text{CH}_3$.
The acid part becomes a sodium carboxylate salt, not the free acid, so count its atoms with Na in place of the acidic H to match one option.
walkthrough:
**Recall alkaline hydrolysis**

Great start, let's remember the pattern. With aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, an ester gives a sodium carboxylate salt plus an alcohol.

$$\text{ester + NaOH} \rightarrow \text{sodium carboxylate + alcohol}$$

**Split ester X into two parts**

Now split $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2(\text{CH}_2)_7\text{CH}_3$ at the ester link. The left side $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ comes from ethanoic acid, the right side $\text{O}(\text{CH}_2)_7\text{CH}_3$ comes from the alcohol.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{R where R = (CH}_2)_7\text{CH}_3$$

**Form the two products**

The acid fragment picks up $\text{Na}^+$ to give sodium ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$. The alcohol fragment picks up H to give octan-1-ol.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na + HO(CH}_2)_7\text{CH}_3$$

**Count atoms for the salt**

Let's count sodium ethanoate carefully. $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ has 2 C, 3 H, 2 O and 1 Na. That is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_3\text{O}_2\text{Na}$, which matches one of the options.

options.A: This is $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, ethanoic acid. That would be the product of acid hydrolysis with dilute acid, not alkaline hydrolysis with NaOH where the acid is neutralised to its sodium salt.
options.B: This is sodium ethanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$. The $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2$ part of ester X forms this salt on reaction with NaOH, so it is a correct product.
options.C: The alcohol product is octan-1-ol, $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{17}\text{OH}$ which is $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}\text{O}$. $\text{C}_8\text{H}_{16}\text{O}$ has two H too few and suggests an aldehyde or ketone, a common counting slip.
options.D: This would be a sodium salt of an 8-carbon acid, as if the ester was reversed. Here the 8-carbon chain is the alcohol part, not the acid part, so no $\text{C}_8$ carboxylate is formed.
